Choosing the root: hand versus code
ID3 picks the attribute whose split removes the most uncertainty, \(IG(S, A) = H(S) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v)\). The tree

The code produces the same tree, read as rules:

IF Previous Grade = Good THEN Pass
IF Previous Grade = Poor AND Assignment = No THEN Fail
IF Previous Grade = Poor AND Assignment = Yes AND Attendance = High THEN Pass
IF Previous Grade = Poor AND Assignment = Yes AND Attendance = Low THEN Fail
IF Previous Grade = Poor AND Assignment = Yes AND Attendance = Medium THEN Pass

title: Who will fail the final exam? An ID3 decision tree, by hand and in code
section: What a 20-row tree can and cannot tell you
text:
What a 20-row tree can and cannot tell you

It fits the training data perfectly (100%), but two leaves rest on one student each. Without held-out data, its real accuracy is unknown.
Greedy splitting can miss useful combinations; study hours never get a say.
Information gain favours many-valued attributes, and ID3 cannot handle continuous values or missing data without help.
Next steps: more cohorts and cross-validation, C4.5 or CART with pruning, numeric features (attendance %, weekly hours), Fail-class recall as the target metric, and a fairness check before any decision about real students.

title: Which chatbot answer will people prefer?
text: Research paper · Advanced HCI

title: Which chatbot answer will people prefer?
text:
The problem
Millions of people now talk to LLM chatbots, but it is still hard to say which of two answers a person will prefer, and why. Human ratings are expensive, LLM-as-a-judge setups are known to favour longer or first-shown answers, and older user-satisfaction models were built for task-oriented dialogue, not open-ended answers.
The Chatbot Arena offers a rare source of real preferences: a user writes a prompt, two anonymous models answer, and the user votes for A, B or a tie. This project turns 57,477 of those votes into a three-class prediction problem and asks a second, HCI question along the way: how much does the presentation of an answer (its length, formatting, refusals) drive what people choose?

title: Which chatbot answer will people prefer?
text:
Approach



The pipeline, from raw Arena battles to the calibrated ensemble.


Data preparation. JSON turns were parsed into text, 187 incomplete battles and 75 duplicates were removed, and the data was split 80/10/10 grouped by prompt, so a popular prompt can never appear in both training and test.
SA-DeBERTa, the proposed model. A DeBERTa-v3-base cross-encoder reads [CLS] prompt [SEP] response A [SEP] response B at once, so self-attention can compare the two answers directly. In parallel, a small MLP embeds 16 style features (log length, word count, line breaks, headings, list items, code blocks and a refusal flag for each answer, plus their length differences). The two representations are concatenated and classified into A / B / tie.
Removing position bias. During training, each battle is shown with A and B swapped (and the label flipped) half of the time; at test time the model scores both orders and averages them. The prediction no longer depends on which answer was shown first.
Calibration. Temperature scaling and a weighted geometric-mean ensemble with the two classical baselines were fitted on the validation set only.

Why style features? Inputs are truncated to 512 tokens, so the encoder cannot see how long a 1,000-word answer really is. In the data, the longer answer won 61.6% of battles with a clear winner. The style branch passes that information explicitly, and keeps it interpretable.

Three things stand out:

SA-DeBERTa beats every single baseline on both log loss and accuracy, and the calibrated ensemble is best overall at 48.4% accuracy, rising to 64.4% when there is a clear winner.
Style is not a detail. With the same encoder and the same training budget, adding the style branch raised accuracy by 3.7 points and swap consistency from 59.7% to 95.9%: the text-only model often changed its mind when the answers were simply shown in the other order.
It was done on modest hardware. Everything, including the transformer, was trained on a single 6 GB laptop GPU, with mixed precision, gradient accumulation and checkpoint/resume runs.


Learning curves
SA-DeBERTa was trained for two epochs in resumable runs with checkpoints every 150 steps (about 80 minutes per epoch on a 6 GB laptop GPU). The final checkpoint was chosen on validation log loss.




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Validation log loss and accuracy during training (1,500-battle validation subset).

title: Which chatbot answer will people prefer?
text:
What drives the predictions?

Length dominates
SHAP values for the LightGBM style model show which presentation features move the predicted preference most. Length differences come first, then the length and structure of each answer, then refusals. Headings barely matter.




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Mean absolute SHAP value per style feature (LightGBM, test set).






A model that learned the users’ bias, and then some

An honest caveat. Users picked the longer answer in 61.6% of battles with a winner. When SA-DeBERTa predicts a winner, it picks the longer one 93.2% of the time, against 63.9% for the text-only model. The style branch helps accuracy precisely because it amplifies the length signal. That is a useful finding for interface designers (presentation shapes judgement), and a warning for anyone who would use such a model as a quality judge.



Where the model succeeds and fails




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Test accuracy by subgroup. Numbers in brackets: battles in the subgroup.




The pattern is consistent across models: accuracy is highest when one answer is much longer or contains a refusal (an easy cue) and lowest when both answers look alike or contain code, where judging quality really needs understanding the content.




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Confusion matrix of the calibrated ensemble, normalised by true class (row %).




Ties are recalled only 32% of the time: a single vote of “tie” can mean both good or both bad, which look nothing alike.

title: Which chatbot answer will people prefer?
text:
What I would do next

Model ties explicitly, for example as separate “both good” and “both bad” outcomes.
Longer context and larger open models on the full Arena data, to see past the 512-token window.
A controlled user study that varies only the length and formatting of the same answer, to separate the causal effect of style from that of content.

title: Which chatbot answer will people prefer?
text:
Reproducibility
The full pipeline (preprocessing, baselines, resumable SA-DeBERTa training, calibration, error analysis and figures) is in the code repository, with a README giving the exact commands. Random seed 42; PyTorch 2.6, Transformers 4.46, scikit-learn 1.9, LightGBM 4.7, SHAP 0.54. Every chart on this page is drawn at build time from the result files that pipeline produced.

Desktop app · Zahrh Esther Hardware Trading LLC, Sharjah, UAE · in daily use since October 2026
A Windows app to write, print, save and track supplier cheques for a hardware trading company. The finance team uses it with real cheque books, real suppliers and real printed cheques, on several office computers sharing one database.

Printing that matches the paper. A cheque layout designer with per-bank offsets (verified on SIB and RAK Bank cheques), range printing, and amounts converted to words.
The whole cheque life cycle: pending, printed, cleared, bounced, stopped, cancelled and spoiled, plus security cheques, received customer cheques, supplier bills and balances, payment vouchers, a calendar view and reports.

Engineering discipline: a pnpm monorepo with pure business rules in their own package (100% test coverage enforced for money, words and dates), database migrations tested in PGlite against every role and function, Row-Level Security in Supabase, and a hardened Electron setup (context isolation, sandbox, no secret keys in the app).

title: Will this order arrive late? Supply chain risk with PySpark
text: In progress · Big Data

title: Will this order arrive late? Supply chain risk with PySpark
text:
Why it matters
A late delivery is rarely a surprise to the data: shipping mode, destination market, product category, order timing and the promised schedule all carry signal. If the risk is known when the order is placed, a company can choose a faster shipping mode, warn the customer, or reorder stock earlier. This is the business problem behind the project.

title: Will this order arrive late? Supply chain risk with PySpark
text:
Why Spark
The dataset is large enough, and wide enough (dozens of columns of mixed types), that a single-machine pandas workflow becomes awkward to repeat and impossible to scale. The project uses Spark the way it would be used on a real cluster: lazy DataFrame transformations, a declared schema, and an MLlib Pipeline whose every step (indexing, encoding, assembling, scaling, modelling) is fitted on training data only and can be re-run on new data unchanged.

title: Will this order arrive late? Supply chain risk with PySpark
text:
The pipeline





flowchart LR
  A[("Raw CSV<br/>DataCo orders")] --> B["Ingest with<br/>explicit schema"]
  B --> C["Clean & dedupe<br/>parse dates"]
  C --> D["Drop leaking<br/>columns"]
  D --> E["Feature engineering<br/>time · market · shipping"]
  E --> F["MLlib Pipeline<br/>StringIndexer → OneHot →<br/>VectorAssembler → Scaler"]
  F --> G["Models<br/>LogReg · RF · GBT"]
  G --> H["CrossValidator<br/>AUC · F1 · recall"]
  H --> I[("Results &<br/>feature importance")]
  classDef done fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#14532D;
  classDef now fill:#FEF3C7,stroke:#D97706,color:#78350F;
  classDef todo fill:#E0E7FF,stroke:#6366F1,color:#1E1B4B;
  class A done; class B now; class C,D,E,F,G,H,I todo;








Problem framing and datasetBinary target: late delivery risk. Business metric: recall on late orders, at a controlled false-alarm rate.


IngestionSpark session, explicit schema (no type inference on a large CSV), basic profiling of every column.


Cleaning and leakage auditColumns only known after shipping (real shipping days, delivery status, shipping date) describe the outcome and must be dropped, or the model learns the answer instead of the risk.


Feature engineeringOrder weekday, month and hour; scheduled shipping days; shipping mode; market, region and country; product category; order value and discount.


MLlib pipelineStringIndexer and OneHotEncoder for categories, VectorAssembler and StandardScaler, fitted on the training split only.


Models and tuningLogistic regression (baseline), Random Forest and Gradient-Boosted Trees, tuned with CrossValidator on a stratified split.


EvaluationROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1 and recall on late orders; feature importance; error analysis by market and shipping mode.


Scaling notesPartitioning, caching and run times, to show what changes when the data no longer fits on one machine.

title: Will this order arrive late? Supply chain risk with PySpark
section: The trap this project is designed to avoid
text:
The trap this project is designed to avoid

Target leakage. In this kind of dataset, some columns are recorded after the parcel has shipped. A model given “actual days for shipping” next to “scheduled days” can reach near-perfect accuracy by subtracting one from the other, and is useless in practice. The audit in step 3 decides, column by column, what is genuinely known at order time. Getting this right matters more than any choice of algorithm.

title: Will this order arrive late? Supply chain risk with PySpark

title: Breast cancer diagnosis: which classifier misses the fewest cancers?
text:
Why this problem needs care
A fine-needle aspirate is imaged and the cell nuclei are measured: radius, texture, area, concavity and so on, each summarised as a mean, a standard error and a “worst” value. The classifier should support, not replace, the pathologist.
The two errors are not equal. A false negative (a cancer labelled benign) can delay treatment; a false positive costs an extra biopsy. So the project optimises for recall on the malignant class without letting specificity collapse, and checks everything with metrics that are not fooled by the 63/37 class split.

title: Breast cancer diagnosis: which classifier misses the fewest cancers?
text:
A leakage-free protocol

Five patients were set aside first (stratified), only to demonstrate final predictions.
The other 564 were split 80/20 with stratification: 451 training, 113 test, both with a 37% malignant rate.
Imputation and scaling live inside scikit-learn pipelines, so their statistics are learned only from the data a model is fitted on. Scaling matters for KNN: feature ranges differ by a factor of more than 200,000.
Each model was tuned with GridSearchCV, 5-fold stratified, scored by malignant-class F1. The test set was used exactly once.

title: Breast cancer diagnosis: which classifier misses the fewest cancers?
section: Results on the shared test set
text:
Results on the shared test set




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Test-set metrics at the default 0.5 threshold (positive class = malignant). Zoomed in: all models are strong.








                            
                                            


Figure 2: Confusion matrices on the 113 test patients (42 malignant, 71 benign).




KNN misses one cancer, the Decision Tree two, the Random Forest three. KNN and the tree tie on accuracy (97.4%); KNN has the best recall, F1, balanced accuracy and MCC. The Random Forest is the interesting case: it is worst at the 0.5 threshold but best at ranking (ROC-AUC 0.997, log loss 0.096). Its boundary is just placed too conservatively, so three cancers fall slightly below the cut-off.

title: Breast cancer diagnosis: which classifier misses the fewest cancers?
text:
Over- and underfitting, made visible




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Validation curves from 5-fold CV on the training set: F1 on the training folds versus the validation folds.




An unrestricted tree reaches a perfect training F1 from depth 7 while validation F1 drops to about 0.90: textbook overfitting, so CV picked depth 5 (amber line). For KNN, k = 1 memorises the training data, large k over-smooths and both curves fall; k = 3 gives the best validation F1 with a small gap.

title: Breast cancer diagnosis: which classifier misses the fewest cancers?
section: Choosing the threshold by the cost of errors
text:
Choosing the threshold by the cost of errors
Assuming a missed cancer costs five times a false alarm (cost = 5·FN + FP), the cheapest KNN threshold was searched using out-of-fold training predictions only.




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Out-of-fold errors and cost for each possible KNN threshold (k = 3 gives probabilities 0, ⅓, ⅔, 1).





What the test set said. Lowering the threshold to 0.33 (malignant if any one of the three neighbours is malignant) was cheapest on the training folds. On the test set it caught no extra cancer (FN stayed at 1) and added 5 false alarms (specificity 97.2% → 90.1%). The default 0.5 was kept for the reported results; 0.33 remains the option for a clinic that values sensitivity above all.

Does the model learn real signal?




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Random Forest feature importance (top 10).




The ranking matches clinical knowledge: malignant nuclei are larger and more irregular. That is reassuring evidence that the models learn the biology, not artefacts.

A borderline case like this should go to the pathologist for a close look, which is exactly how such a tool should be used.

title: Breast cancer diagnosis: which classifier misses the fewest cancers?
text:
Limits, stated plainly

With 42 malignant test cases, one patient moves recall by 2.4 points; KNN and the tree are within each other’s CV standard deviation.
One institution, early 1990s: performance on other equipment and populations is unknown.
With k = 3, KNN probabilities are coarse and poorly calibrated (log loss 0.365 vs 0.096 for the Random Forest). If calibrated risk scores were needed, the Random Forest wins.
The 5:1 cost ratio is an assumption, to be agreed with clinicians.
